snapshot.title: Constitutional Bodies: ECI, CAG, UPSC & Finance Commission
snapshot.exam_hook: 🏔️ UPSC Ranker Hook: ECI: Art 324. CAG: Art 148. UPSC: Art 315. FC: Art 280. SPSC members removed by PRESIDENT only. CAG cannot hold office after retirement.

quick_notes.title: Election Commission (Art 324)
quick_notes.detail: Conducts elections to Parliament, State Legislatures, and offices of President/VP. (Note: State Election Commission conducts local body polls). Multi-member body (1 CEC + 2 ECs). CEC has security of tenure like a SC judge (removed by impeachment). ECs can be removed by President on recommendation of CEC.
quick_notes.explanation: Article 324 of the Constitution of India establishes the Election Commission, which is the independent authority that runs elections for

quick_notes.title: Comptroller and Auditor General (Art 148)
quick_notes.detail: "Guardian of the Public Purse". Audits accounts of Union and States. Appointment by President for 6 years or 65 years age. Security of tenure like SC judge. Salary/conditions cannot be varied to disadvantage. Not eligible for further office under Government after retirement.
quick_notes.explanation: Comptroller and Auditor General, often called CAG, is a constitutional authority mentioned in Article 148 of the Indian Constitution. The CAG is called the Guardian of the Public Purse because its main job is to check and verify, which is called auditing, all the money records and accounts of the Union government and the State governments. The CAG is appointed by the President of India and serves for a term of 6 years, or until he or she reaches the age of 65 years, whichever comes first. The CAG has security of tenure, meaning he or she cannot be removed easily, and this protection is similar to that of a Supreme Court (SC) judge. The salary and service conditions of the CAG are fixed by law and cannot be changed in a way that puts the CAG at a disadvantage. After retirement, the CAG is not eligible for any further office or job under the Union or any State government.

quick_notes.title: UPSC & SPSC (Art 315–323)
quick_notes.detail: UPSC: Central recruiting agency. Members appointed by President. Security of tenure (removed by President only on SC inquiry for misbehaviour). Advisory role (advice not binding). SPSC : State level. Members appointed by Governor but REMOVED ONLY BY PRESIDENT.
quick_notes.explanation: The UPSC, which stands for the Union Public Service Commission, is the central recruiting agency for the central government, meaning it hires people for all-India and central civil services. Its members are appointed by the President of India, and they have security of tenure, which means they cannot be easily removed; a member can only be removed by the President if a Supreme Court (SC) inquiry finds them guilty of misbehaviour. The UPSC has an advisory role, so when it gives advice to the government, that advice is not binding, meaning the government does not have to follow it. The SPSC, which stands for the State Public Service Commission, is the same kind of agency but for a single state, so it hires people for that state's civil services. Its members are appointed by the Governor of that state, but they can only be removed by the President of India, not by the Governor. These rules are found in Articles 315 to 323 of the Constitution, which lay out the setup and powers for both the UPSC and the SPSC.

quick_notes.title: Finance Commission (Art 280)
quick_notes.detail: Quasi-judicial body. 1 Chairman + 4 Members appointed by President every 5 years. Recommends : 1. Vertical Devolution (Centre to States). 2. Horizontal Devolution (Between States). 3. Grants-in-aid. Recommendations are ADVISORY (not binding). 15th FC (N.K. Singh) recommended 41% share for states.
quick_notes.explanation: Finance Commission (Article 280) The Finance Commission is a body set up by the President of India every five years to decide how tax money should be shared between the central government and the state governments. It has one Chairman and four other members, all appointed by the President. This body is called a quasi-judicial body because it works like a court to make fair recommendations, but it is not an actual court. The Commission gives advice on three main things: first, the vertical devolution, which is the percentage of central taxes that should go to all states combined; second, the horizontal devolution, which is how that total share is divided among individual states based on factors like population and poverty; and third, grants-in-aid, which are extra payments from the centre to help poorer states. These recommendations are advisory, meaning the government does not have to follow them, but in practice they are usually accepted. The 15th Finance Commission, chaired by N.K. Singh, recommended that states receive 41% of all central tax revenue.

topic_title: Constitutional Bodies: ECI, CAG, UPSC & Finance Commission
lesson_intro: Constitutional Bodies are the 'Pillars of Indian Democracy'. These institutions derive their authority directly from the Constitution, giving them a high degree of independence from the government of the day. Today we study the 'Big Four': the Election Commission of India (ECI), the Comptroller and Auditor General (CAG), the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC), and the Finance Commission. For a UPSC aspirant, understanding their 'Security of Tenure' and 'Functions' is vital, as these bodies are the gatekeepers of fair elections, financial accountability, and meritocracy in the civil services.
